title: Unit 2f - Shallow vs. Deep Copies and 2D Allocation
summary: Title slide introducing the unit on shallow vs. deep copy and 2D allocation in C++, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 2f - Shallow vs. Deep Copies and 2D Allocation. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This unit covers the distinction between shallow and deep copies of data in C++, as well as techniques for dynamically allocating 2D array structures using arrays of pointers.
notes_text: Opening slide establishing the two major topics: copy semantics (shallow vs. deep) and 2D dynamic allocation patterns in C/C++.

metadata.topic: Shallow vs. Deep Copy and 2D Allocation

title: Shallow vs. Deep Copy - Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the shallow vs. deep copy topic.
main_text: This is a section divider slide introducing the topic of Shallow vs. Deep Copy. The following slides will explore what it means to copy pointers versus copying the underlying data, and why the distinction matters for correct memory management in C++.
notes_text: Transition slide separating the shallow vs. deep copy section from the rest of the unit.

title: Fixed Size Arrays Are Limited
summary: Shows the limitation of fixed-size 2D char arrays for storing variable-length strings at runtime.
main_text: Task: Store 10 names that are NOT known until the program runs (runtime) and could be short or long. Approach 1: Fixed size (static) arrays. This approach uses a 2D char array like char names[10][20], allocating 10 rows of 20 characters each. The problem is that this is bad because it either wastes space (for short names like 'Tim Lee') or some user will enter a string just a little too long (e.g. 'Christopher Alexander-Johnson'). Fixed-size arrays cannot adapt to the actual length of runtime input. The code shown includes #include <iostream>, #include <cstring>, using namespace std, and declares char names[10][20] inside main().
notes_text: This motivates the need for dynamic memory allocation. A fixed 2D array wastes memory for short strings and risks buffer overflow for long strings. This limitation drives the introduction of pointer-based variable-size arrays.

images.description: A 2D grid diagram showing names[10][20] with rows indexed 0, 1, ..., 2 and columns 0 through 19, illustrating fixed-size character storage where each row has the same number of slots regardless of actual string length.

title: Variable Size Arrays
summary: Introduces variable-size arrays using an array of pointers, each pointing to a differently-sized string, forming a jagged array.
main_text: Task: Store 10 names that are NOT known until the program runs (runtime) and could be short or long. Approach 2: Variable-size arrays. Use arrays that are 'just the right size' for each string. Use an array of pointers to point at each string. The type of names is char* names[10], which is an array of 10 char pointers. Each pointer (names[0], names[1], etc.) points to a separately allocated character array of the exact length needed. For example, names[0] points to 'Tim\0' (4 chars), names[1] points to 'Christopher\0' (12 chars), names[2] points to 'Maya\0' (5 chars), and names[9] points to 'Shohei\0' (7 chars). Having a collection of different-size arrays is sometimes referred to as 'JAGGED ARRAYS'. What type is names? It is char** (a pointer to pointer to char).
notes_text: The key insight is that char* names[10] gives us 10 pointers, each of which can independently point to a char array of any length. This flexibility avoids both wasted space and overflow. The term 'jagged array' describes the irregular row lengths.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a char** names array at address 2840 with entries [0] through [9]. Each entry is a char* pointer pointing to a separately allocated character array of different length: 'Tim\0' at 2130 (4 bytes), 'Christopher\0' at 2610 (12 bytes), 'Maya\0' at 2380 (5 bytes), 'Shohei\0' at 1950 (7 bytes). This illustrates the jagged array concept.

metadata.topic: Variable Size Arrays and Jagged Arrays

title: Reading in the Input [1]
summary: Asks whether directly reading into uninitialized char* pointers will work, showing the initial flawed approach.
main_text: Approach 2: Variable-size arrays. Use arrays that are 'just the right size' for each string. Use an array of pointers to point at each string. Will the code to the right work to read in the 10 strings? The code declares char* names[10] and then loops: for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { cin >> names[i]; }. The question is whether this code correctly reads 10 strings into the names array. The diagram shows the names array with entries [0] through [9], each containing a char* pointer, but no allocated memory is shown for these pointers to point to.
notes_text: This slide sets up the problem: the array of pointers exists, but each pointer does not yet point to any valid memory. The next slide reveals why this fails.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char** names array at address 2840 with entries [0] through [9], each containing a char* pointer with no memory allocated for it to point to, illustrating uninitialized pointers.

title: Reading in the Input [2]
summary: Reveals that reading into uninitialized char* pointers fails because no memory is allocated; pointers point to nothing.
main_text: Approach 2: Variable-size arrays. Use arrays that are 'just the right size' for each string. Use an array of pointers to point at each string. Will the code to the right work to read in the 10 strings? No!!! You had 10 pointers (addresses) but do you own any memory? And what do those 10 pointers point to? NOTHING!! The code char* names[10] followed by cin >> names[i] does not work because the pointers are uninitialized. Each names[i] contains a garbage address (shown as '??') and the arrows point to question marks, meaning they reference invalid or unknown memory locations. Writing to these addresses causes undefined behavior.
notes_text: Critical concept: declaring an array of pointers does NOT allocate the memory those pointers should point to. Each char* is uninitialized and contains a garbage value. Attempting cin >> names[i] writes to an arbitrary memory location, which is undefined behavior and typically crashes.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char** names array with entries [0] through [9]. Each entry contains '??' (garbage addresses) with arrows pointing to large question marks, illustrating that no valid memory is allocated for these pointers to reference.

title: Chicken and the Egg
summary: Explains the input-before-allocation dilemma and proposes using a temporary fixed-size buffer as a scratchpad.
main_text: Issue: I can't get the input without owning ('renting') memory, but I don't know how much memory to 'rent' since I don't know the input. Options: Best Option: Use what we are doing (did) in HW2 (Variable-length array problem) where we grow the array as we read in data. Alternative: Make 1 FIXED SIZE array as LARGE as we might ever need and use it as a scratchpad for reading in our data. The alternative approach declares char temp_buf[40], a temporary (scratchpad) buffer of 40 characters for receiving the input. This fixed buffer is large enough for any reasonable input. After reading into the buffer, we can determine the string length and allocate exactly the right amount of memory.
notes_text: The 'chicken and egg' problem is fundamental to dynamic string handling: you need to know the size before allocating, but you need to read the data to know the size. The scratchpad buffer solution reads into a fixed temporary buffer first, then performs a deep copy to properly sized storage.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char** names array with uninitialized char* entries on the left, and a separate char temp_buf[40] array on the right with indices 0 through 39 and empty slots, labeled as a temporary (scratchpad) buffer for receiving input.

title: Copy That!
summary: Shows a flawed attempt to copy input from temporary buffer to names array using pointer assignment instead of data copying.
main_text: Plan: Read in each name to the temporary input buffer. Copy the input from the temporary buffer to its own storage and set the pointer to that storage. Does the code on the right work? The code declares char myInput[40] as scratch/temporary storage. In a loop for(int i=0; i < 10; i++), it reads cin >> myInput, then assigns names[i] = myInput. The question is whether this approach correctly stores each name independently. The diagram shows myInput at address 2000 as a 40-character buffer, and the names array with uninitialized char* pointers.
notes_text: This sets up the shallow copy problem. The code uses simple pointer assignment (names[i] = myInput) rather than allocating new memory and copying the string data. The next slide reveals why this is incorrect.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char* myInput buffer at address 2000 with 40 slots, and char** names array at address 2840 with entries [0] through [9] containing uninitialized char* pointers. The code attempts names[i] = myInput.

title: That's Shallow!
summary: Reveals that assigning names[i] = myInput only copies the pointer address, not the data, creating a shallow copy where all entries point to the same buffer.
main_text: Plan: Read in each name to the temporary input buffer. Copy the input from the temporary buffer to its own storage and set the pointer to that storage. Does the code on the right work? No!! What is being copied? Just the start address! The code names[i] = myInput copies only the pointer value (address 2000) into each names[i]. After the loop, all 10 entries (names[0] through names[9]) contain the same address 2000, meaning they all point to the same single myInput buffer. We are ONLY copying pointers and NOT the underlying data! This is known as a SHALLOW COPY (i.e. copying the pointer but not the data pointed at).
notes_text: This is the central definition of shallow copy: only the pointer (address) is duplicated, not the data it references. All 10 names entries end up pointing to the exact same memory location (address 2000), so they all see whatever the last input was. This is a fundamental bug pattern in C/C++.

images.description: Memory diagram showing all entries names[0] through names[9] containing the same address 2000, with red arrows all pointing to the single myInput buffer at address 2000. A red box at the bottom states: 'We are ONLY copying pointers and NOT the underlying data! This is known as a SHALLOW COPY (i.e. copying the pointer but not the data pointed at)'.

title: To Each Their Own
summary: Explains that each string needs its own dynamically allocated storage, motivating the use of dynamic allocation with new.
main_text: We need each new input string to have its own storage. We need 10 char arrays, not just 1! And they must be variable length. So, we need to use DYNAMIC ALLOCATION! The code still uses char* names[10] and char myInput[40], reads cin >> myInput, but the line names[i] = myInput is crossed out (marked as wrong). The diagram shows the correct result: names[0] points to address 2130 containing 'Tim\0', names[1] points to 2610 containing 'Christopher\0', names[2] points to 2380 containing 'Maya\0', and names[9] points to 1950 containing 'Shohei\0'. Each string has its own separately allocated memory.
notes_text: This slide bridges the gap between the shallow copy problem and the deep copy solution. The key realization is that we need 10 separate char arrays, each dynamically allocated to the correct size, rather than one shared buffer.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char** names array where each entry points to a uniquely allocated char array: names[0]->2130 'Tim\0', names[1]->2610 'Christopher\0', names[2]->2380 'Maya\0', names[9]->1950 'Shohei\0'. The line names[i] = myInput is crossed out with a prohibition symbol.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [1]
summary: Introduces the three steps of a deep copy and demonstrates step 1: determining the size of data to copy using strlen.
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). This slide shows iteration i=0 of the loop. After reading 'Tim' into myInput (at address 2000), the code computes int len = strlen(myInput), which returns 3. The names array entries still contain garbage '??' values. This is step 1: measuring the length of the string we need to copy.
notes_text: strlen returns the number of characters excluding the null terminator. We will need len+1 bytes to store the string including its null terminator. This measurement step is essential because we must know the exact size before allocating.

images.description: Memory diagram at i=0 showing myInput buffer at address 2000 containing 'Tim\0' followed by unused space. The expression int len = strlen(myInput) => 3 is highlighted. The names array entries still show '??' values.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [2]
summary: Demonstrates step 2 of deep copy: dynamically allocating a new char array of the correct size using new char[len+1].
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). This slide highlights step 2: Dynamic allocation. At i=0, after determining len=3 from strlen, the code executes names[i] = new char[len + 1]. This allocates 4 bytes (len+1 to include the null terminator) on the heap and stores the returned address (2130) in names[0]. The diagram shows names[0] now pointing to address 2130, which has 4 empty slots (indices 0, 1, 2, 3) ready to receive the copied data.
notes_text: The +1 in new char[len+1] is critical: strlen returns the count without the null terminator, but we must allocate space for it. Forgetting the +1 causes a buffer overrun when strcpy copies the null terminator.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names[0] now holding address 2130, pointing to a newly allocated 4-byte array at address 2130 with empty slots. The expression names[i] = new char[len + 1] is highlighted. Other names entries still show '??'.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [3]
summary: Demonstrates step 3 of deep copy: explicitly copying data using strcpy to transfer the string into newly allocated memory.
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). This slide highlights step 3: Explicitly copying the data. At i=0, the code executes strcpy(names[i], myInput), which copies the string 'Tim\0' from the myInput buffer at address 2000 into the newly allocated array at address 2130. After the copy, names[0] points to 2130 which now contains 'T', 'i', 'm', '\0'. The arrow shows data flowing from myInput down into the allocated array.
notes_text: strcpy copies characters one by one from source to destination, including the null terminator. This completes the deep copy for the first iteration. The data now exists independently in its own allocated memory, separate from the temporary buffer.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the strcpy operation. An arrow flows from myInput (containing 'Tim\0' at address 2000) down into the allocated array at address 2130, which now contains 'Tim\0'. The expression strcpy(names[i], myInput) is highlighted.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [4]
summary: Shows that after a deep copy, the temporary buffer can safely be overwritten with the next input without affecting previously stored data.
main_text: Now we can get the next input and overwrite the input string, since we just made a deep copy of it to its own array. At i=1, the loop reads the next name into myInput. Since names[0] has its own independent copy of 'Tim\0' at address 2130, overwriting myInput with the next input does not affect the previously stored name. The diagram shows names[0] pointing to 2130 containing 'Tim\0', while the other entries (names[1] through names[9]) still contain garbage '??' values, ready to be populated in subsequent iterations.
notes_text: This demonstrates the key benefit of deep copy: once the data has been copied to its own allocated memory, the original source (myInput buffer) can be freely reused. The stored data is completely independent.

images.description: Memory diagram at i=1 showing names[0] pointing to 2130 containing 'Tim\0' (safely stored), myInput buffer still showing 'Tim\0' but about to be overwritten, and names[1] through names[9] still containing '??' values.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [5]
summary: Shows the second iteration reading 'Christopher' into myInput and computing strlen to get length 11.
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). At i=1, the loop reads 'Christopher' into myInput at address 2000. Step 1 repeats: int len = strlen(myInput) returns 11. The diagram shows myInput now containing 'Christopher\0' and names[0] still safely pointing to its own copy of 'Tim\0' at address 2130. The remaining names entries still contain '??'.
notes_text: The three-step deep copy process repeats for each iteration. 'Christopher' is 11 characters, so we will need 12 bytes (len+1) for the allocation in the next step.

images.description: Memory diagram at i=1 showing myInput containing 'Christopher\0' at address 2000, with int len = strlen(myInput) => 11 highlighted. names[0] points to 2130 with 'Tim\0', other entries show '??'.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [6]
summary: Shows step 2 of the second iteration: allocating 12 bytes for 'Christopher' and storing the new address in names[1].
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array. At i=1, step 2: names[i] = new char[len + 1] allocates 12 bytes (11 characters + null terminator) on the heap. The returned address 2610 is stored in names[1]. The diagram shows names[0] pointing to 2130 ('Tim\0'), names[1] now pointing to 2610 (a new 12-slot empty array at indices 0-11), and remaining entries still '??'.
notes_text: Each iteration allocates exactly the right amount of memory. 'Tim' needed 4 bytes, 'Christopher' needs 12 bytes. The jagged array structure naturally emerges from these differently-sized allocations.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names[1] now holding address 2610, pointing to a newly allocated 12-byte array with empty slots at indices 0-11. names[0] still points to 2130 with 'Tim\0'.

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [7]
summary: Shows step 3 of the second iteration: strcpy copies 'Christopher' into the newly allocated array at names[1].
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). At i=1, step 3: strcpy(names[i], myInput) copies 'Christopher\0' from the myInput buffer at address 2000 into the allocated array at address 2610. The diagram shows the completed copy with names[0] pointing to 2130 ('Tim\0') and names[1] pointing to 2610 ('Christopher\0'). An arrow shows data flowing from myInput down into the allocated array at 2610.
notes_text: After this step, both 'Tim' and 'Christopher' are independently stored in their own memory. The process continues for all 10 names.

images.description: Memory diagram showing strcpy copying 'Christopher\0' from myInput at address 2000 into the array at address 2610. Arrow shows data flow. names[0]->2130 'Tim\0', names[1]->2610 'Christopher\0'.
labels: C h r i s t o p h e r \0

title: Go Deep: Deep Copy [8]
summary: Shows the final state after all 10 iterations of deep copy, with each name stored in its own dynamically allocated array.
main_text: A 'deep copy' usually requires 3 steps: 1) Determine the size of the data to copy (if it's not known). 2) Dynamic allocation of an array of that size. 3) Explicitly copying the data to the new array (usually with some kind of loop or strcpy()). At i=9 (the last iteration), the loop reads 'Shohei' into myInput and completes the deep copy process. The final code is: for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { cin >> myInput; int len = strlen(myInput); names[i] = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(names[i], myInput); }. The completed diagram shows all entries populated: names[0]->2130 'Tim\0', names[1]->2610 'Christopher\0', names[2]->2380 'Maya\0', names[9]->1950 'Shohei\0'. Each name has its own independently allocated storage.
notes_text: The complete deep copy loop performs all three steps (measure, allocate, copy) for each iteration. The result is a jagged array where each string occupies exactly the memory it needs, and all strings are independent of each other and of the temporary buffer.

images.description: Final memory diagram at i=9 showing all names entries populated: names[0]->2130 'Tim\0', names[1]->2610 'Christopher\0', names[2]->2380 'Maya\0', names[9]->1950 'Shohei\0'. myInput at 2000 contains 'Shohei\0'. Each pointer leads to its own separate array.

title: Summary: Deep vs. Shallow
summary: Side-by-side comparison defining shallow copy as copying only pointers and deep copy as allocating new storage and copying data.
main_text: SHALLOW COPY: Copying pointers but NOT the underlying data pointed at. This leads to many references/pointers to the same data. The shallow copy diagram shows all 10 names entries containing address 2000, all pointing to the single myInput buffer. DEEP COPY: Creating whole new storage and then copying the underlying data into that new storage. Generally requires dynamic allocation and some work (a loop) to copy the data. The deep copy diagram shows each names entry pointing to its own unique address (2130, 2610, 2380, 1950) with independently stored strings ('Tim\0', 'Christopher\0', 'Maya\0', 'Shohei\0').
notes_text: This is the key summary slide for the shallow vs. deep copy distinction. Shallow copy creates aliases (multiple pointers to same data), while deep copy creates independent copies. Deep copy requires three steps: determine size, allocate, and explicitly copy. Understanding this distinction is fundamental for correct memory management in C/C++.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison diagrams. Left side (SHALLOW COPY): all names entries point to the same myInput buffer at address 2000 with red arrows converging. Right side (DEEP COPY): each names entry points to a uniquely allocated array containing an independent copy of each string, with separate arrows to different addresses.

title: Use it; Don't Lose It
summary: Emphasizes that after deep copy, you can use the data but must retain pointers for eventual memory cleanup.
main_text: You can now use the data. But don't lose your pointers since we need to eventually clean up. The code shows the complete program: after the deep copy loop (cin >> myInput, int len = strlen(myInput), names[i] = new char[len + 1], strcpy(names[i], myInput)), there is a print loop: for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { cout << names[i] << endl; }. The diagram shows the completed state with myInput containing 'Shohei\0' at address 2000, and all names entries pointing to their respective independently allocated strings. The key message is that every 'new' must eventually have a matching 'delete' to prevent memory leaks.
notes_text: Losing a pointer to dynamically allocated memory means that memory can never be freed, causing a memory leak. The next slides will cover proper cleanup (deallocation) of the dynamically allocated strings.

images.description: Complete memory diagram showing all names entries pointing to their allocated strings, with myInput still containing 'Shohei\0'. The code includes both the deep copy loop and a print loop using cout.

title: Clean Up! [1]
summary: Poses the question of how many delete operations are needed to match the 10 new operations performed during deep copy.
main_text: How many new operations did we do? 10. So, how many delete operations do we need to perform? The code shows the complete program with the deep copy loop (new char[len + 1] called 10 times), a print loop, and a comment section for 'Clean up'. The question highlights the fundamental rule of memory management: every 'new' must be matched by a corresponding 'delete'. Since we allocated 10 separate char arrays, we need 10 delete[] operations. The diagram shows all the allocated arrays with pointers from the names array.
notes_text: The rule is simple: count your 'new' operations and ensure you have the same number of 'delete' operations. In this case, the loop ran 10 times calling 'new' each time, so we need a loop running 10 times calling 'delete[]' each time.

images.description: Memory diagram showing all 10 names entries pointing to their allocated strings (Tim, Christopher, Maya, Shohei shown), illustrating the 10 separate allocations that need corresponding deallocations.

title: Clean Up! [2]
summary: Shows the cleanup code using a loop of delete[] operations to free all 10 dynamically allocated string arrays.
main_text: How many new operations did we do? 10. So, how many delete operations do we need to perform? 10. The cleanup code uses a loop: for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { delete [] names[i]; }. This iterates through each pointer in the names array and deallocates the memory it points to. The diagram shows each allocated string array being crossed out with a prohibition symbol and labeled with 'delete [] names[0]', 'delete [] names[1]', 'delete [] names[2]', and 'delete [] names[9]', indicating each is being freed. After this cleanup, all the dynamically allocated memory is returned to the system.
notes_text: The delete[] syntax (with square brackets) is required because each allocation used new char[...] (array form). Using delete without brackets on array allocations causes undefined behavior. The cleanup loop mirrors the allocation loop structurally.

images.description: Memory diagram showing each allocated string being crossed out with prohibition symbols. Labels 'delete [] names[0]', 'delete [] names[1]', 'delete [] names[2]', 'delete [] names[9]' appear next to each array being freed.

title: Updating our Data [1]
summary: Poses the question of how to replace a name in the array, showing a flawed approach using direct pointer assignment.
main_text: Suppose we now wanted to replace one (or more) of the names (e.g. 'Tim' => 'Allie'). What do you think of the code to the right? The code reads the replacement name into myInput (getting 'Allie'), then assigns names[0] = myInput. This is the same shallow copy mistake from before. The diagram shows myInput at address 2000 now containing 'Allie\0', while the original allocated arrays still exist: names[0] previously pointed to 2130 ('Tim\0'), names[1] to 2610 ('Christopher\0'), etc.
notes_text: This revisits the shallow copy problem in the context of updating data. Simply assigning names[0] = myInput creates a shallow copy and introduces additional problems including a memory leak.

images.description: Memory diagram showing myInput containing 'Allie\0' at address 2000, with names[0] still pointing to 2130 ('Tim\0'). The code names[0] = myInput is highlighted as the replacement attempt.

title: Leaking Data
summary: Reveals that the shallow copy replacement causes a memory leak because the old 'Tim' allocation is orphaned with no pointer.
main_text: Suppose we now wanted to replace one (or more) of the names (e.g. 'Tim' => 'Allie'). No, this is a shallow copy. Even worse, does anyone have a pointer to 'Tim'? No, memory leak! After names[0] = myInput, names[0] now holds address 2000 (pointing to myInput buffer) instead of 2130. The original allocation at address 2130 containing 'Tim\0' is now orphaned: no pointer references it, so it can never be freed. This is a memory leak. The red-highlighted 'Tim\0' at address 2130 is shown disconnected from any pointer, illustrating the leak.
notes_text: This slide demonstrates two problems with the shallow copy approach for updates: (1) names[0] now points to the temporary buffer instead of owned memory, and (2) the memory at address 2130 allocated for 'Tim' is leaked because no pointer can reach it anymore. The old memory must be deleted before reassigning the pointer.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names[0] now containing 2000 (pointing to myInput) instead of 2130. The array at address 2130 containing 'Tim\0' is highlighted in red, disconnected from any pointer, illustrating the memory leak.

metadata.topic: Memory Leak from Shallow Copy Update

title: Updating our Data [2]
summary: Considers reusing the existing array for the new name by reading directly into the old allocation, but this approach has size issues.
main_text: Suppose we now wanted to replace one (or more) of the names (e.g. 'Tim' => 'Allie'). What about this code where we just reuse the same array we already have? The code reads the replacement directly into the existing allocation: cin >> names[0] (reading 'Allie'). The diagram shows names[0] pointing to address 2130, where 'Allie\0' has been written over the old 'Tim\0' content. Since 'Tim' was 3 characters and the allocation was 4 bytes (len+1), but 'Allie' is 5 characters needing 6 bytes, this writes beyond the allocated 4 bytes, causing a buffer overrun.
notes_text: While reusing the existing array might seem efficient, it fails when the new string is longer than the old one. The original allocation was sized for 'Tim' (4 bytes), but 'Allie' needs 6 bytes, causing a buffer overflow that overwrites adjacent heap memory.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names[0] pointing to address 2130, where 'Allie\0' has been written into the 4-byte allocation that was originally sized for 'Tim'. The 'e' and null terminator extend beyond the allocated bounds.

title: Repeat: Deep Copy [1]
summary: Introduces the correct approach to update: perform a deep copy by allocating new memory for the replacement string.
main_text: Suppose we now wanted to replace one (or more) of the names (e.g. 'Tim' => 'Allie'). We need to perform a DEEP COPY. Are we forgetting anything? The code reads 'Allie' into myInput, then performs: int len = strlen(myInput); names[0] = new char[len + 1]; strcpy(names[0], myInput). The diagram shows names[0] now updated from 2130 to 2748, pointing to a new allocation at address 2748 containing 'Allie\0'. However, the old 'Tim\0' at address 2130 is still shown, and the question 'Are we forgetting anything?' hints that the old memory needs to be freed first.
notes_text: This approach correctly allocates new memory and copies the data, but it still has the memory leak problem: the old allocation at 2130 ('Tim') was not freed before names[0] was reassigned. The next slide addresses this.

images.description: Memory diagram showing names[0] changed from 2130 to 2748, pointing to new allocation at 2748 with 'Allie\0'. The old 'Tim\0' at 2130 is still shown but disconnected, hinting at a memory leak.

title: Repeat: Deep Copy [2]
summary: Shows the complete correct update procedure: first delete the old allocation, then allocate new memory and copy the replacement data.
main_text: Suppose we now wanted to replace one (or more) of the names (e.g. 'Tim' => 'Allie'). We need to perform a DEEP COPY. But first, delete the old copy. The correct update sequence is: 1) delete [] names[0] to free the old 'Tim' allocation. 2) int len = strlen(myInput) to measure the new string. 3) names[0] = new char[len + 1] to allocate new memory. 4) strcpy(names[0], myInput) to copy the new data. The diagram shows 'Tim\0' at address 2130 being crossed out with a prohibition symbol (deleted), and names[0] updated to 2748 pointing to the new allocation containing 'Allie\0'. The code highlights delete [] names[0] as the critical first step before reassignment.
notes_text: The complete update procedure requires four steps: delete old memory, measure new size, allocate new memory, copy new data. Forgetting the delete causes a memory leak. This pattern (delete-then-reallocate) is essential whenever replacing dynamically allocated data through a pointer.

images.description: Memory diagram showing 'Tim\0' at address 2130 crossed out with a prohibition symbol (freed via delete), and names[0] now pointing to 2748 containing 'Allie\0'. The delete [] names[0] line is highlighted in the code.

title: 2D Array Allocation - Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the 2D array allocation topic.
main_text: This is a section divider slide introducing the topic of 2D Array Allocation. The following slides will cover how to dynamically allocate and manage 2D array structures in C/C++ using arrays of pointers, since the language does not natively support dynamic multi-dimensional array allocation.
notes_text: Transition slide separating the 2D array allocation section from the shallow/deep copy section. The 2D allocation topic builds on the pointer and dynamic allocation concepts established earlier.

title: Arrays of Pointers - Motivation
summary: Motivates arrays of pointers by showing the pain of managing multiple related 1D arrays separately without a unifying structure.
main_text: We often want to have several arrays to store data, such as storing each student's grades. Those arrays may be related (i.e. scores of students in a class). Yes, a 2D array would probably have been better in this case (int scores[4][5]), but suppose we already had a bunch of these 1D arrays. How can I access them easily? The 'Painful' code declares four separate arrays: int s1[5] = {0,0,0,0,0}, int s2[5], int s3[5], int s4[5]. It then uses four separate for loops to sum each array into avg, which is repetitive and hard to maintain. The code also shows the four arrays at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800, each containing 5 zero-initialized integers.
notes_text: This slide establishes the problem: when you have multiple related 1D arrays, accessing and processing them requires duplicated code for each array. An array of pointers provides a way to treat them uniformly using loops with indexing.

images.description: Four separate 1D arrays labeled s1=240, s2=300, s3=480, s4=800, each containing 5 zeros. The code shows four separate for loops (one per array), labeled 'Painful'.

title: Arrays of Pointers - Solution
summary: Shows how an array of pointers collects multiple 1D arrays into a single indexable structure, effectively forming a 2D array.
main_text: We can make an array of pointers where each entry points at an array of integers (of a student's scores). This effectively forms a 2D array. Fact: An array of pointers is how a 2D array is often represented. The improved code declares int *scores[4] = {s1, s2, s3, s4}, creating an array of 4 pointers. Each pointer references one of the existing 1D arrays. The 'Better' code uses nested loops: for(int i=0; i < 4; i++) { int avg = 0; for(int k=0; k < 5; k++) { avg += scores[i][k]; } cout << avg / 5.0 << endl; }. The diagram shows scores at address 500 containing [0]=240, [1]=300, [2]=480, [3]=800, with arrows pointing to each 1D array. Using scores[i][k] syntax provides 2D-array-style access.
notes_text: The key insight is that scores[i][k] works because scores[i] returns a pointer to a 1D array, and [k] then indexes into that array. This double-indexing gives the same syntax as a true 2D array. The array of pointers is the fundamental building block for dynamic 2D allocation.

images.description: Diagram showing scores array at address 500 with 4 entries containing addresses 240, 300, 480, 800. Arrows point from each entry to the corresponding 1D array (s1, s2, s3, s4), each with 5 zeros. This illustrates how an array of pointers forms a 2D structure.

title: Arrays of Pointers - Dynamic Allocation Need
summary: Shows that when array sizes are unknown at compile time, static declarations fail and dynamic allocation is required.
main_text: What if the number of students and the number of scores for each student are NOT KNOWN until the program runs. Are the options shown to the right legal in C++? No, I need dynamic allocation! The code shows int numStu, numScores; cin >> numStu >> numScores;. Then it asks: is int scores[numStu][numScores] okay in C++? No, variable-length arrays are not standard in C++. Is int s1[numScores] = {0,0,0,0,0}; int s2[numScores] = {0,0,0,0,0}; okay? No, because we don't even know how many of these to allocate since numStu is a variable. The conclusion is that dynamic allocation is needed.
notes_text: C++ does not support variable-length arrays (VLAs) as part of the standard (unlike C99). Even if a compiler supports VLAs as an extension, you still cannot create a variable number of separate array declarations. Dynamic allocation with new is the correct solution.

title: Allocating a 2D Array Structure [1]
summary: Explains that C/C++ does not support direct 2D dynamic allocation, but supports allocating 1D arrays and 1D arrays of pointers separately.
main_text: Fact: Sadly, C/C++ does NOT easily support dynamic allocation of 2D-, 3D-, etc. arrays of variable size. The syntax int** scores = new int[numStu][numScores] is BAD and does not work. BUT, C/C++ does support dynamic allocation of 1D arrays AND 1D arrays of pointers. So, I can try to allocate separate 1D arrays (1 array per row), but how can I 'collect' or put all the separate 1D arrays together into a single 2D array? The code shows the loop: for(int i=0; i < numStu; i++) { ?? = new int[numScores]; }. The ?? placeholder asks what variable should receive the pointer returned by new. The diagram shows 4 separate 1D arrays at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800, each with 5 question mark entries.
notes_text: The key limitation is that new only allocates 1D arrays. To simulate a 2D array, you must allocate an array of pointers (one per row) and then allocate each row separately. The ?? in the code is answered in the next slide: it is scores[i].

images.description: Diagram showing 4 separate dynamically allocated 1D arrays at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800, each with 5 uninitialized entries (question marks). The arrays are not yet connected to any pointer structure.

title: Allocating a 2D Array Structure
summary: Shows the complete 2D allocation pattern: allocate an int** array of row pointers, then allocate each row as an int array.
main_text: Fact: Sadly, C/C++ does NOT easily support dynamic allocation of 2D-, 3D-, etc. arrays of variable size. By allocating a 1D array of pointers, it would need to be dynamically allocated since the number of rows (numStu) is a variable. That dynamic allocation of an array of int*s would return an int**. The complete code: int** scores = new int*[numStu]; allocates an array of numStu pointers. Then for(int i=0; i < numStu; i++) { scores[i] = new int[numScores]; } allocates each row. The diagram shows int** scores at address 500, pointing to an array of 4 pointers at address 500: [0]=240, [1]=300, [2]=480, [3]=800. Each pointer leads to a 1D array of 5 question marks.
notes_text: The two-step allocation pattern is: (1) allocate the array of row pointers with new int*[numStu], returning int**, and (2) allocate each row with new int[numScores], returning int*. The int** type arises because it is a pointer to an array of int* values.

images.description: Diagram showing int** scores pointing to address 500, which contains a 4-element pointer array. Each element points to a separate 1D array of 5 question marks at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800. Labels show the two-level structure.

title: Initializing a 2D Array Structure
summary: Shows that dynamically allocated arrays contain garbage values and must be explicitly initialized, typically using nested loops.
main_text: Beware, any data you allocate is just garbage values. You'd need to initialize the data somehow (likely with another loop). The code shows the complete allocation and initialization: int** scores = new int*[numStu]; for(int i=0; i < numStu; i++) { scores[i] = new int[numScores]; for(int k=0; k < numScores; k++) { scores[i][k] = 0; // or cin >> scores[i][k]; } }. The nested loop first allocates each row, then initializes each element to 0 (or reads from input). The diagram shows the completed structure with int** scores at address 500, each row pointer leading to a 1D array of five zeros.
notes_text: Unlike stack-allocated arrays which may be zero-initialized in some contexts, heap-allocated memory (from new) always contains garbage. The nested loop pattern (outer for rows, inner for columns) is the standard way to initialize a dynamically allocated 2D structure.

images.description: Diagram showing the completed 2D structure with int** scores at address 500 pointing to 4 rows. Each row contains 5 zeros (0 0 0 0 0) at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800, showing properly initialized data.

title: Deallocating a 2D Array Structure [1]
summary: Shows the first step of 2D deallocation: deleting each row array before deleting the pointer array, mirroring the allocation.
main_text: Be sure to deallocate all the memory. The structure used to deallocate memory should be a MIRROR of the code used to allocate with new. The code shows allocation followed by a deallocation loop: for(int i=0; i < numStu; i++) { delete [] scores[i]; }. This frees each individual row array. The diagram shows each row array (at addresses 240, 300, 480, 800) being crossed out with prohibition symbols, indicating they are being freed. However, the pointer array (scores itself at address 500) is not yet freed.
notes_text: Deallocation must happen in reverse order of allocation: first free the rows (which were allocated second), then free the pointer array (which was allocated first). Deleting the pointer array first would lose access to the row pointers, causing memory leaks.

images.description: Diagram showing each row array crossed out with prohibition symbols (freed). The pointer array at address 500 still exists with entries 240, 300, 480, 800. Only the rows are freed so far.

title: Deallocating a 2D Array Structure [2]
summary: Shows the complete 2D deallocation: after deleting all rows, delete the pointer array itself with delete [] scores.
main_text: Be sure to deallocate all the memory. The structure used to deallocate memory should be a MIRROR of the code used to allocate with new. The complete deallocation code: for(int i=0; i < numStu; i++) { delete [] scores[i]; } followed by delete [] scores;. The first loop frees each row array, and then delete [] scores frees the pointer array itself. The diagram shows all row arrays crossed out (freed) and the pointer array also being freed. After both steps, all dynamically allocated memory has been returned to the system. The deallocation mirrors the allocation: allocate pointer array first, then rows; deallocate rows first, then pointer array.
notes_text: The complete deallocation pattern for a dynamic 2D array requires exactly N+1 delete operations: N deletes for the rows plus 1 delete for the pointer array. This mirrors the N+1 new operations during allocation. Forgetting the final delete [] scores would leak the pointer array.

images.description: Diagram showing all row arrays and the pointer array crossed out with prohibition symbols, indicating complete deallocation. Both levels of the 2D structure are freed.

title: 2D Allocation: Repeated Example
summary: Complete worked example of dynamic 2D array allocation, initialization, access, and deallocation with concrete memory addresses.
main_text: Dynamically allocating 2D arrays in C/C++ doesn't really work. Instead conceive of 2D array as an 'array of arrays' which boils down to a pointer to a pointer. To allocate an N row x M column array dynamically we: Allocate an array of N pointers. Allocate each row of M columns separately and have each of the N pointers point to a different row. The code shows: int *t = new int[n][m]; // DOESN'T WORK!! The correct approach: int **t = new int*[n]; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { t[i] = new int[m]; for(int j = 0; j < m; j++) { t[i][j] = 0; } }. Access elements as t[r][c] as desired. Deallocation: for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { delete t[i]; } delete [] t;. The example uses a 3x4 matrix with values [[0,7,2,1],[1,16,31,20],[8,14,5,0]]. The diagram shows t at address 410, pointing to a pointer array with entries [0]=1a0, [1]=2c0, [2]=1b4. Each pointer leads to a row: 1a0->[0,7,2,1], 2c0->[1,16,31,20], 1b4->[8,14,5,0]. t[2] = 0x1b4 and t[2][1] = 0.
notes_text: This comprehensive example shows every step of the 2D dynamic allocation lifecycle: failed attempt with new int[n][m], correct two-step allocation, nested initialization, element access with double indexing, and proper two-step deallocation. Note that the deallocation of rows should use delete[] (with brackets) since each row is an array.

images.description: Memory diagram showing t (int**) at address 410 pointing to pointer array with entries 1a0, 2c0, 1b4. Each entry points to a row: 1a0->[0,7,2,1], 2c0->[1,16,31,20], 1b4->[8,14,5,0]. Annotations show t[2]=0x1b4 and t[2][1]=0. A 3x4 matrix is shown separately with the same values.

main_text: In-class-exercises: nxmboard. Students are directed to complete the nxmboard exercise, which practices dynamically allocating, using, and deallocating a 2D array structure of variable size (N rows by M columns).
